title: A day to play, a place to belong: Jordan’s children celebrate World Children’s Day
subtitle: Hundreds of children gathered at Amman’s Children’s Museum for an inclusive celebration of learning, friendship and the right to play.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: For 10-year-old Ayman Bawab, the request was simple: more days like this. “I wish we could have days like this more often. I got to play, make things and meet new friends,” he told UNICEF.

Ayman was among hundreds of children who came together at the Children’s Museum in Amman on 18 November for a UNICEF-organised celebration ahead of World Children’s Day. Participants came from across Jordan’s governorates and included refugees, children with disabilities and children from Gaza, according to the organisation.

Hands-on activities and live performances made space for children to learn, create and spend time together. The occasion put a welcome subject at the centre of the news: children enjoying themselves, with opportunities to join in.

World Children’s Day, marked on 20 November, commemorates the adoption of the Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1989. Its promise includes protection and education, but also rest, leisure, play and participation in cultural life. Article 31 asks governments to encourage equal opportunities for recreation and the arts. A day of discovery belongs within that promise.

The setting matters. Opened in 2007, the Children’s Museum is a place built around learning through play. Its regular attractions invite children to investigate the world rather than simply look at objects behind glass.

The museum describes exhibits covering flight, mathematics, light and astronomy. A tinkering studio encourages visitors to invent, try things and learn from attempts that do not work. There are also an art studio, a library and a garden. These are the museum’s ongoing offerings; they should not be confused with a verified programme of what every child did at this week’s event.

For families, the appeal is easy to recognise: a shared place where a child can ask questions, make something or discover an unfamiliar interest. Children need not produce an impressive result for the experience to be worthwhile. Having time to explore is part of the point.

The more demanding question is how such opportunities reach children who cannot easily get to the museum or afford a visit. The institution’s Museum for All initiative, launched in 2010, explicitly aims to reduce financial and geographical barriers.

Its Mobile Museum, operating since 2012, offers free visits for families and students in the communities it reaches. The museum also describes free school visits through its partnership with UNRWA and free entry for public-school students during school terms under its arrangement with Jordan’s education ministry.

Another outreach programme, Science Everywhere, takes interactive science shows into settings including hospitals, refugee camps, host communities and schools. The museum says it is designed with children who have spent time out of school in mind. That work gives the celebration a practical context: there are ways to bring discovery closer to children, as well as invite children into a building.

These programmes do not establish that every child can participate. Nor can one joyful gathering resolve interrupted education, inaccessible facilities or the pressures facing displaced families. The available event report does not measure lasting educational or psychological outcomes, and a celebration should not be asked to stand in for that evidence.

What it can offer is a moment in which children are recognised for their curiosity, friendships and wishes. Listening to those wishes is itself part of taking children seriously. Ayman’s hope for more days together leaves adults with a useful task: make room for play beyond the annual celebration.
